topics.name: Noble gases
topics.kicker: Group 18 of the periodic table · The unreactive gases with full shells
topics.briefing: The noble gases are the elements in the far-right column of the periodic table: helium, neon, argon, krypton, xenon, radon, and the human-made oganesson. Their outer electron shells are full, so they almost never react, which is why they were once called the “inert” gases. That calm makes them useful: helium lifts balloons, argon protects the glowing filaments of old-style light bulbs, and neon glows red-orange in signs.
topics.answerHtml: Noble gases (accept group 18, group VIIIA, or group 0 elements, or inert gases; prompt on group 8)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In 1962, Neil Bartlett made the first compound of one of these elements after realizing that xenon gives up an electron almost as easily as an oxygen molecule does. The two lightest members of this group form no known stable compounds under ordinary conditions.
tossups.r: These elements sit in the last column of the periodic table. For 10 points, name this group of very unreactive elements, including helium and neon.

tossups.p: In 1785, Henry Cavendish sparked air with extra oxygen and was left with a tiny bubble of gas that refused to react, later identified as one of these elements. Over a century later, Lord Rayleigh noticed that nitrogen taken from air was slightly denser than nitrogen made from chemicals.
tossups.r: Rayleigh and William Ramsay then discovered argon. For 10 points, name this group of unreactive elements that also includes neon and xenon.

tossups.p: In 1898, William Ramsay and Morris Travers found three of these elements in liquefied air and named them from Greek words meaning “new,” “hidden,” and “stranger.” Another member’s name comes from the Greek word for “lazy.”
tossups.r: These elements almost never react because their outer shells are full. For 10 points, name this group of elements, which includes neon, krypton, and xenon.

tossups.p: From 1960 to 1983, the meter was officially defined by the wavelength of an orange-red light given off by krypton-86, an isotope of one of these elements. Another of these elements, xenon, powers the ion engines of some spacecraft, such as NASA’s Dawn probe.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this unreactive group of elements on the far right side of the periodic table.

tossups.p: The heaviest member of this group was named for Yuri Oganessian [“oh-gah-ness-YAHN”] in 2016, making him only the second person to have an element named for him during his lifetime. Like the names of neon, argon, krypton, and xenon, that element’s name ends in “-on.”
tossups.r: Most of these elements are colorless, odorless gases. For 10 points, name this group of elements whose atoms have full outer electron shells.

tossups.p: Most of the argon in Earth’s atmosphere was made by the radioactive decay of potassium-40, a process geologists use to date volcanic rocks. Argon, the most common member of this group in air, makes up almost 1 percent of the atmosphere.
tossups.r: Atoms of these elements have full outer shells. For 10 points, name this group of elements, which includes helium, neon, and argon.

tossups.p: Excimer lasers, used in some eye surgeries and in making computer chips, rely on short-lived molecules that join one of these elements, such as argon or krypton, to fluorine. Mixed with neon, helium produces the red beam of a common gas laser.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this group of elements that rarely react because their outer electron shells are full.

tossups.p: In each of the first six rows of the periodic table, the highest first ionization energy belongs to a member of this group, and one member has the highest ionization energy of any element. Their atoms attract one another only through weak London dispersion forces, so their boiling points are very low.
tossups.r: Neon and argon belong to this group. For 10 points, name this group of elements just to the right of the halogens.

tossups.p: Georges Claude [“zhorzh KLOHD”] displayed the first glowing tubes filled with one of these elements at a show in Paris in 1910. In such signs, that element glows red-orange, while argon mixed with a little mercury gives a blue glow.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this group of elements, including neon and argon, in the far-right column of the periodic table.

tossups.p: Dmitri Mendeleev’s [“men-duh-LAY-efs”] original periodic table had no place for these elements, so a whole new column was added after William Ramsay discovered several of them in the 1890s. Ramsay won the 1904 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for finding them.
tossups.r: Chemists once called these elements “inert.” For 10 points, name this group of unreactive elements, including krypton and radon.

tossups.p: Chemists shorten long electron configurations by writing the symbol of one of these elements in square brackets, as in [Ne] 3s¹ for sodium. Other atoms often gain, lose, or share electrons until they match the arrangement of one of these elements.
tossups.r: That idea is the octet rule. For 10 points, name this group of elements with full outer shells, including helium and argon.

tossups.p: Friedrich Ernst Dorn reported in 1900 that radium gives off one of these elements as a radioactive gas. That member, the heaviest that occurs in nature, forms when uranium in soil and rocks decays, so homes are sometimes tested for it.
tossups.r: That gas is radon. For 10 points, name this group of elements, which also includes xenon and neon.

tossups.p: In 2000, chemists in Finland made the first neutral compound of argon, a molecule with hydrogen and fluorine that survives only at extremely low temperatures. Unlike most gases, the members of this group exist as single atoms rather than as molecules.
tossups.r: They are found in the rightmost column of the periodic table. For 10 points, name this group of elements, which includes argon and krypton.

tossups.p: Because they do not react, members of this group fill old-style light bulbs so the hot tungsten filament will not burn up, and they shield hot metal from the air during welding. Their group name compares them to gold and platinum, metals that also resist reacting.
tossups.r: Neon and xenon are members. For 10 points, name this group of elements whose outer electron shells are full.

tossups.p: Going down this group, boiling points rise as the atoms grow larger and easier to distort, and the lightest member has the lowest boiling point of any element. That lightest member has only two valence electrons, while the others have eight.
tossups.r: These elements very rarely form compounds. For 10 points, name this group of elements that includes helium, neon, and xenon.

trap.title: The family, not one member
trap.body: Tossups on this group are full of single-member clues, like neon signs, helium balloons, argon in light bulbs, and radon in basements, which tempt players to blurt one element’s name. But the question wants the whole family. The halogens, one column to the left, are the other trap: they are among the most reactive elements, while this group almost never reacts.
trap.fix: Listen for “these elements” or “this group,” and answer with the family name. Full outer shells, single atoms, Bartlett’s xenon compound, and Ramsay’s discoveries mean this group; seven valence electrons, salts, and −1 ions mean the halogens.
trap.line: Real answer line: Noble gases (accept group 18, group VIIIA, or group 0 elements, or inert gases; prompt on group 8)

topics.name: Ideal gas law
topics.kicker: PV = nRT · How a gas’s pressure, volume, and temperature are linked
topics.briefing: The ideal gas law ties together four things you can measure about a gas: its pressure, its volume, its temperature, and how many moles of it there are. Written PV = nRT, it combines older laws discovered by Robert Boyle, Jacques Charles, and Amedeo Avogadro. It describes an imaginary “ideal” gas whose particles take up no space and never attract one another, yet real gases such as air follow it closely under everyday conditions.
topics.answerHtml: Ideal gas law (accept PV = nRT or ideal gas equation; prompt on gas law)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: For a gas that obeys this law exactly, the molar heat capacity at constant pressure minus the molar heat capacity at constant volume equals this law’s constant, a result called Mayer’s relation. Such a gas does not change temperature when it expands freely into a vacuum.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law relating a gas’s pressure, volume, temperature, and number of moles.

tossups.p: Émile Clapeyron [“klah-pay-RAWN”] first stated this law in 1834 by combining earlier laws named for Robert Boyle and Jacques Charles. In its modern form, this law also includes Avogadro’s law through a term for the number of moles.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law often summarized as pressure times volume equals moles times R times temperature.

tossups.p: Johannes van der Waals won the 1910 Nobel Prize in Physics for an equation that corrects this law, using one constant for the attractions between molecules and another for the space the molecules take up.
tossups.r: Real gases obey this law poorly at high pressures and low temperatures. For 10 points, name this law relating pressure, volume, moles, and temperature.

tossups.p: A gas’s compressibility factor compares its actual pressure-volume product with the value this law predicts, and it equals exactly 1 for a gas that obeys this law. At a temperature called the Boyle temperature, a real gas follows this law well over a wide range of pressures.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this equation of state that combines Boyle’s law, Charles’s law, and Avogadro’s law.

tossups.p: Writing this law in terms of the number of molecules instead of moles replaces its usual constant with the Boltzmann constant. That usual constant, about 8.314 joules per mole per kelvin, is called the gas constant and is written R.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law that relates the pressure, volume, temperature, and amount of a gas.

tossups.p: The kinetic molecular theory explains this law by assuming that gas particles take up no volume, never attract or repel one another, and bounce off each other in perfectly elastic collisions. Real gases follow this law best at high temperatures and low pressures.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this gas law, written with the letters P, V, n, R, and T.

tossups.p: Rearranging this law shows that a gas’s density depends on its molar mass, so chemists can find an unknown gas’s molar mass by measuring its density. This law predicts that one mole of any gas at 0 degrees Celsius and 1 atmosphere fills about 22.4 liters.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law, which combines the simpler gas laws into one equation with the constant R.

tossups.p: Daniel Bernoulli’s 1738 book _Hydrodynamica_ explained gas pressure as the result of countless tiny particles hitting the walls of their container, an early step toward explaining this law. In this law, temperature must be measured in kelvins, starting from absolute zero.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law that combines Boyle’s law and Charles’s law with Avogadro’s law.

tossups.p: The internal energy of a gas that perfectly obeys this law depends only on its temperature, so such a gas would show no Joule–Thomson effect, the temperature change of a gas forced through a valve. Real gases differ from this law because their molecules attract one another and take up space.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law, which states that pressure times volume equals moles times the gas constant times temperature.

tossups.p: For a reversible adiabatic process, a gas obeying this law keeps the product of its pressure and its volume raised to the power gamma constant, where gamma is the ratio of its heat capacities. At constant temperature, this law reduces to Boyle’s law.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this gas law that relates pressure, volume, temperature, and the number of moles.

tossups.p: Guillaume Amontons [“ah-mohn-TOHN”] noticed long before Gay-Lussac that a gas’s pressure rises with its temperature when its volume is held fixed, a rule built into this law. According to this law, heating the air inside a hot-air balloon makes that air less dense, so the balloon rises.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law relating pressure, volume, temperature, and the number of moles of a gas.

tossups.p: Constant-volume gas thermometers rely on this law, and extending straight-line graphs of a gas’s volume against its temperature down to zero volume points to absolute zero, about −273 degrees Celsius. In 1802, Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac published measurements showing that different gases expand by the same fraction when heated, a finding built into this law.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this gas law, in which temperature must be measured in kelvins rather than degrees Celsius.

tossups.p: The virial [“VEER-ee-ul”] equation of state adds a series of correction terms to this law, which is the first term of that series. Since 2019, this law’s constant has had an exact value, because the Avogadro and Boltzmann constants were fixed exactly.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law, whose constant R is about 0.0821 liter-atmospheres per mole per kelvin.

tossups.p: Dalton’s law of partial pressures can be derived from this law for mixtures of gases, since each gas pushes in proportion to its number of moles. No real gas obeys this law perfectly, because real molecules have size and attract one another, though helium comes very close.
tossups.r: Its constant, R, is called the gas constant. For 10 points, name this law relating a gas’s pressure, volume, temperature, and amount.

tossups.p: In a gas that obeys this law, the average translational kinetic energy of a molecule is three-halves times the Boltzmann constant times the temperature. At constant pressure, this law says that doubling a gas’s kelvin temperature doubles its volume.
tossups.r: Chemists use it to relate a gas’s pressure, volume, and temperature. For 10 points, name this law that combines Boyle’s, Charles’s, and Avogadro’s laws.

clues.t: Pressure times volume equals moles times the gas constant R times temperature
Combines Boyle’s law, Charles’s law, and Avogadro’s law (plus Gay-Lussac’s law)
Temperature must be measured in kelvins, starting from absolute zero
Its constant R is about 8.314 joules per mole per kelvin, or 0.0821 liter-atmospheres per mole per kelvin
Describes a hypothetical gas whose particles take up no space and never attract one another
Real gases follow it best at high temperature and low pressure and stray from it at high pressure and low temperature
Johannes van der Waals corrected it with one constant for attractions and one for molecule size (1910 Nobel Prize in Physics)
Kinetic molecular theory explains it: tiny particles in random motion with perfectly elastic collisions
One mole of gas at 0 degrees Celsius and 1 atmosphere fills about 22.4 liters
Written for molecules instead of moles, its constant becomes the Boltzmann constant
Émile Clapeyron first stated it in 1834, combining Boyle’s and Charles’s laws
Rearranged, it lets chemists find a gas’s molar mass from its density
Heated air at constant pressure becomes less dense, so hot-air balloons rise
Dalton’s law of partial pressures can be derived from it for gas mixtures
The compressibility factor compares a gas’s actual pressure-volume product with its prediction; it equals exactly 1 for a gas that obeys it
At the Boyle temperature, a real gas obeys it well over a wide range of pressures
It is the simplest equation of state; the virial equation adds a series of correction terms to it
Mayer’s relation: a gas’s molar heat capacities at constant pressure and at constant volume differ by its constant R
Its internal energy depends only on temperature, so it shows no temperature change expanding into a vacuum and no Joule–Thomson effect
In a reversible adiabatic process, pressure times volume raised to the power gamma stays constant
Daniel Bernoulli’s 1738 _Hydrodynamica_ explained gas pressure as particles hitting the walls of their container
Guillaume Amontons noticed long before Gay-Lussac that pressure rises with temperature at a fixed volume
In 1802, Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac showed that different gases expand by the same fraction when heated
Constant-volume gas thermometers rely on it; extending volume-temperature lines to zero volume points to absolute zero, about −273 degrees Celsius
A molecule’s average translational kinetic energy is three-halves the Boltzmann constant times the temperature
Since 2019, its constant R has an exact value, because the Avogadro and Boltzmann constants were fixed
No real gas obeys it perfectly, but helium comes very close

trap.title: Whole law, not a piece
trap.body: This law is built from simpler gas laws, so its clues often mention Boyle’s law (pressure and volume), Charles’s law (volume and temperature), or Avogadro’s law (volume and moles). Those are separate answer lines, and so is the gas constant, R, which is only one part of this equation. The combined gas law is a trap too: it links pressure, volume, and temperature but leaves out the number of moles.
trap.fix: If the clues include all four quantities, the constant R, real-gas corrections like van der Waals’s, or the kinetic molecular theory’s assumptions, answer with the full law. A few tossups ask for the imaginary gas itself, the “ideal gas,” which is also accepted.
trap.line: Real answer line: Ideal gas law (accept PV = nRT or ideal gas equation; prompt on gas law)

topics.name: Enthalpy
topics.kicker: A system’s heat content · Its change shows if a reaction gives off heat
topics.briefing: Enthalpy, written H, is a system’s heat content; chemists can’t measure its total amount, so they measure its change, ΔH: the heat a reaction gives off or soaks up at constant pressure. A campfire has a negative ΔH because it releases heat (exothermic), while an instant cold pack has a positive ΔH because it absorbs heat (endothermic). In 1840, Germain Hess showed that the total change is the same no matter how many steps a reaction takes.
topics.answerHtml: Enthalpy (or H; accept change in enthalpy or delta H; prompt on heat or heat content)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Heike Kamerlingh Onnes [“KAH-mer-ling ON-us”], better known for discovering superconductivity, is credited with coining the name of this quantity. Chemists can measure only changes in this quantity, never its total amount, so data tables list its standard changes of formation instead.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this thermodynamic quantity, a system’s heat content, whose change is negative in exothermic reactions.

tossups.p: When a gas squeezes through a porous plug or a narrow valve in a Joule–Thomson expansion, this quantity stays the same, an effect used to cool gases until they turn into liquids. For an ideal gas, this quantity depends only on temperature.
tossups.r: At constant pressure, its change equals the heat that flows in or out. For 10 points, name this quantity used to classify reactions as exothermic or endothermic.

tossups.p: Heat capacity at constant pressure is defined as the rate at which this quantity changes with temperature. Citrus farmers spray their trees with water on freezing nights because water gives off heat as it freezes, a process with a negative change in this quantity.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this state function whose change is negative when a reaction gives off heat.

tossups.p: The thermite reaction between aluminum powder and iron oxide, used to weld railroad tracks, has such a large negative change in this quantity that it produces glowing, melted iron. In the equation for Gibbs free energy, temperature times the change in entropy is subtracted from the change in this quantity.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity, whose change is positive for endothermic reactions that absorb heat from their surroundings.

tossups.p: The Clausius–Clapeyron [“klah-pay-RAWN”] equation uses a liquid’s change in this quantity on vaporizing to predict how its vapor pressure rises with temperature. Water has an unusually large change in this quantity for vaporizing, which is why evaporating sweat cools the skin.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this thermodynamic quantity, a system’s heat content, whose changes of fusion and vaporization are absorbed when solids melt and liquids boil.

tossups.p: The van ’t Hoff [“vahnt HOFF”] equation shows that how much an equilibrium constant shifts with temperature depends on the standard change in this quantity. By Le Chatelier’s [“luh shah-tuh-LYAY”] principle, heating a reaction with a negative change in this quantity pushes its equilibrium back toward the reactants.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity whose change, usually given in kilojoules per mole, is negative for exothermic reactions.

tossups.p: The Born–Haber cycle adds up steps such as turning solid sodium into a gas and splitting chlorine molecules into atoms to calculate the lattice energy of sodium chloride. That cycle relies on a law of constant heat summation about this quantity.
tossups.r: Germain Hess published that law in 1840. For 10 points, name this quantity, a system’s heat content, whose total change does not depend on a reaction’s path.

tossups.p: A sealed bomb calorimeter measures a reaction’s change in internal energy, but a foam coffee-cup calorimeter, open to the air at constant pressure, measures the change in this quantity directly. Burning one mole of methane changes this quantity by about negative 890 kilojoules.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity, whose change is negative in exothermic reactions such as combustion.

tossups.p: Chemists can estimate a reaction’s change in this quantity by adding up the energies of the bonds that break and subtracting the energies of the bonds that form. A reaction that forms stronger bonds than it breaks has a negative change in this quantity.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this thermodynamic quantity, the heat content of a system at constant pressure.

tossups.p: Elements in their standard states, such as oxygen gas and graphite, have a standard change of formation of zero for this quantity. A reaction’s change in this quantity can be found by subtracting the reactants’ standard values of formation from the products’ values.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity, whose change equals the heat a reaction absorbs or releases at constant pressure.

tossups.p: On a heating curve, the flat sections show a substance absorbing the change in this quantity needed to melt or boil while its temperature stays the same. Instant cold packs feel cold because dissolving ammonium nitrate in water has a positive change in this quantity.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity, whose change is positive for endothermic processes and negative for exothermic ones.

tossups.p: Any strong acid mixed with any strong base releases about the same heat per mole of water formed, so those reactions share nearly the same negative change in this quantity. A reaction that has a negative change in this quantity and a positive change in entropy is spontaneous at every temperature.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity, whose change is negative for heat-releasing reactions like burning wood.

tossups.p: Germain Hess’s 1840 law says the change in this quantity for a reaction is the same whether the reaction happens in one step or many, because this quantity is a state function that depends only on the starting and ending states.
tossups.r: Reactions that lower this quantity give off heat. For 10 points, name this quantity, a system’s total heat content.

tossups.p: Hand warmers heat up because the rusting of iron powder inside them has a large negative change in this quantity. On an energy diagram for an exothermic reaction, the products sit lower than the reactants because they have less of this quantity.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity, whose change tells whether a reaction is exothermic or endothermic.

tossups.p: Adding the product of pressure and volume to internal energy gives this quantity, which chemists find useful because most lab reactions happen open to the air at constant pressure. Under those conditions, its change equals the heat, q, that flows into or out of a system.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity whose change is negative for exothermic reactions, such as burning fuels.

clues.t: A system’s heat content; its change equals the heat absorbed or released at constant pressure
Its change is negative for exothermic reactions (heat released) and positive for endothermic reactions (heat absorbed)
Its change is written with a capital Greek delta (Δ) and usually measured in kilojoules per mole
Combustion, such as burning wood or methane, has a large negative change because it gives off heat
Hess’s law: its total change is the same no matter how many steps a reaction takes
A state function: its change depends only on the starting and ending states, not on the path
Defined as internal energy plus pressure times volume (U + PV)
Its standard change of formation is zero for elements in their standard states, like oxygen gas or graphite
A reaction’s change = formation values of the products minus formation values of the reactants
Estimated from bond energies: energy of bonds broken minus energy of bonds formed
A coffee-cup calorimeter measures its change at constant pressure; a sealed bomb calorimeter measures internal energy instead
In the Gibbs free energy equation, temperature times the entropy change is subtracted from its change
Dissolving ammonium nitrate in water has a positive change, which is why instant cold packs feel cold; hand warmers use rusting iron
Its changes of fusion and vaporization are absorbed during melting and boiling, the flat parts of a heating curve
Burning one mole of methane changes it by about −890 kilojoules
Heike Kamerlingh Onnes, who discovered superconductivity, is credited with coining its name
Stays constant in a Joule–Thomson expansion through a porous plug or valve, which is used to cool and liquefy gases
For an ideal gas, it depends only on temperature
Heat capacity at constant pressure is the rate at which it changes with temperature
Citrus farmers spray their trees with water on freezing nights, because water gives off heat as it freezes (a negative change)
The thermite reaction of aluminum and iron oxide, used to weld railroad tracks, has such a large negative change that it melts the iron it makes
The Clausius–Clapeyron equation uses its change of vaporization to relate vapor pressure and temperature
Water’s unusually large change for vaporizing is why evaporating sweat cools the skin
The van ’t Hoff equation: how an equilibrium constant shifts with temperature depends on its standard change
Le Chatelier’s principle: heating a reaction with a negative change pushes its equilibrium back toward the reactants
The Born–Haber cycle uses Hess’s law to find the lattice energy of ionic solids like sodium chloride
Any strong acid neutralizing any strong base releases about the same heat per mole of water formed, so all have nearly the same negative change
A negative change plus a positive entropy change makes a reaction spontaneous at every temperature

trap.title: Not entropy, not “heat”
trap.body: This quantity and entropy sound alike and sit side by side in the Gibbs free energy equation, so players swap them. Entropy (S) measures how spread out energy is, often called disorder, while this quantity (H) measures heat content. Saying just “heat” only earns a prompt, and an early buzz on a Gibbs clue might want Gibbs free energy itself.
trap.fix: Exothermic, endothermic, Hess’s law, calorimeters, heats of formation, and bond energies mean this quantity. Disorder, the second law of thermodynamics, and the Boltzmann constant mean entropy. If the question asks for the quantity that tells whether a reaction is spontaneous, that is Gibbs free energy.
trap.line: Real answer line: Enthalpy (or H; accept change in enthalpy or delta H; prompt on heat or heat content)

topics.name: Colloids
topics.kicker: Tiny particles spread through another substance · Milk, fog, and gelatin
topics.briefing: A colloid is a mixture whose particles are much bigger than most molecules but still too small to see or to settle out, so they stay spread through another substance, as in milk, fog, whipped cream, and gelatin. Shine a flashlight through one and the beam lights up, because the particles scatter light, a trick called the Tyndall effect. Scottish chemist Thomas Graham named them in 1861 from the Greek word for “glue.”
topics.answerHtml: Colloids (accept colloidal dispersions or colloidal suspensions; prompt on heterogeneous mixtures or dispersions; do not accept “suspension” or “solution” alone)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Richard Zsigmondy [“ZHIG-mon-dee”] won the 1925 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for studying these mixtures, using an ultramicroscope he helped invent to see light scattered by their particles. That instrument let scientists count particles far too small for an ordinary microscope.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these mixtures, such as milk, fog, and gelatin, whose particles are too small to settle out but large enough to scatter light.

tossups.p: The Svedberg won the 1926 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for studying these mixtures, inventing the ultracentrifuge to make their tiny particles settle. Jean Perrin [“zhahn peh-RAN”] won the Physics Nobel the same year, partly for experiments on how particles in these mixtures settle and jiggle.
tossups.r: That jiggling is called Brownian motion. For 10 points, name these mixtures, like milk and fog, whose particles stay spread out instead of settling.

tossups.p: Thomas Graham, who also has a law about how fast gases effuse, named these mixtures in 1861 from the Greek word for “glue.” Graham used membranes to separate them from dissolved salts, a process called dialysis that he pioneered.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these mixtures, such as mayonnaise and whipped cream, which fall between solutions and suspensions in particle size.

tossups.p: Butter and milk are both emulsions, a kind of these mixtures, but butter holds water droplets in fat, while milk holds fat droplets in water. Adding salt can make the particles in many of these mixtures clump together, a process called flocculation or coagulation.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these mixtures, like fog and gelatin, whose particles scatter a beam of light in the Tyndall effect.

tossups.p: The Roman Lycurgus [“lye-KUR-gus”] Cup looks green in reflected light and red when lit from behind, because its glass is one of these mixtures, holding tiny particles of gold and silver. In 1857, Michael Faraday made a ruby-red example containing tiny gold particles.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these mixtures whose particles are too small to settle out, such as milk and fog.

tossups.p: River deltas form partly because fine clay particles spread through river water clump together when they meet salty seawater. Electrostatic precipitators clean smoke, one of these mixtures, out of factory chimneys by giving its tiny particles an electric charge and then collecting them on metal plates.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these mixtures whose particles, between about 1 and 1,000 nanometers across, scatter light in the Tyndall effect.

tossups.p: Because the particles in many of these mixtures carry electric charge, they drift toward an electrode in an electric field, a process called electrophoresis. Those particles usually all carry the same kind of charge, so they repel each other instead of clumping together.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these mixtures, which include emulsions, foams, and gels, whose particles never settle out.

tossups.p: Chemists sort these mixtures into lyophilic [“lye-oh-FIL-ik”] types, whose particles attract the liquid around them, and lyophobic types, whose particles do not. In water treatment, alum is added to make these mixtures of dirt particles clump and sink.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these mixtures, like milk, whose particles stay spread out instead of settling and make a flashlight beam visible.

tossups.p: Above a certain concentration, soap molecules gather into balls called micelles [“my-SELLZ”], forming “association” types of these mixtures. Egg yolk helps make mayonnaise one of these mixtures by keeping drops of oil spread through a watery liquid.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these mixtures, whose types include emulsions and aerosols, that scatter light in the Tyndall effect.

tossups.p: Some of these mixtures are thixotropic [“thik-suh-TROP-ik”], becoming runnier when they are shaken or stirred and thickening again at rest. In a gel, one type of these mixtures, a liquid is trapped inside a network of solid particles or strands.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these mixtures, including gelatin, whose particles are larger than those in solutions but smaller than those in suspensions.

tossups.p: No gas-in-gas type of these mixtures exists, because gases always mix evenly into a solution. Smoke is one of these mixtures with solid particles spread through a gas, while fog spreads liquid droplets through a gas, and both are called aerosols.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these mixtures, like milk and whipped cream, whose particles do not settle out over time.

tossups.p: The random jiggling of particles in these mixtures is named for botanist Robert Brown, who watched tiny bits from pollen grains doing it in water in 1827. Albert Einstein explained that jiggling in 1905 as the result of collisions with moving molecules.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these mixtures, such as fog and milk, that scatter light in the Tyndall effect.

tossups.p: NASA’s Stardust spacecraft caught comet dust in aerogel, a super-light solid made by drying one type of these mixtures. Marshmallows, pumice, and plastic foam cups are “solid foam” examples of these mixtures, with gas bubbles trapped in a solid.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these mixtures, which also include emulsions like milk and mayonnaise.

tossups.p: Unlike the particles in a suspension, the particles in these mixtures pass through ordinary filter paper, but much finer membranes can trap them. Milk is one of these mixtures called an emulsion, and homogenizing it breaks its butterfat into smaller droplets so the cream does not rise.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these mixtures, like fog and gelatin, that fall between solutions and suspensions in particle size.

tossups.p: Each of these mixtures has a dispersed phase spread through a continuous phase called the dispersion medium. Many paints and inks are sols, the type of these mixtures with solid particles in a liquid, while gelatin and jelly are gels.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these mixtures, like milk and fog, that scatter a beam of light in the Tyndall effect.

clues.t: A mixture with tiny particles spread through another substance that never settle out
Examples include milk, fog, whipped cream, mayonnaise, and gelatin
Their particles scatter a beam of light, like headlights in fog: the Tyndall effect
Their particles are bigger than those in a solution but smaller than those in a suspension
Particles are about 1 to 1,000 nanometers across
Made of a dispersed phase spread through a continuous phase called the dispersion medium
Emulsions are liquid in liquid, like milk and mayonnaise; in mayonnaise, egg yolk keeps oil drops spread through water
Foams are gas in liquid (whipped cream, shaving cream); solid foams are gas in solid (marshmallows, pumice)
Aerosols are liquid or solid particles in a gas: fog and clouds (liquid) and smoke (solid)
Gels trap a liquid in a solid network (gelatin, jelly); sols have solid particles in a liquid (many paints and inks)
No gas-in-gas type exists, because gases always mix evenly into a solution
Their particles jiggle randomly in Brownian motion, named for Robert Brown, who saw it in 1827
Named in 1861 by Thomas Graham, from the Greek word for “glue”
Their particles pass through ordinary filter paper but can be trapped by much finer membranes
Thomas Graham, of Graham’s law of effusion, pioneered dialysis, using membranes to separate them from dissolved salts
Richard Zsigmondy helped invent the ultramicroscope and won the 1925 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for studying them
1926 Nobels: The Svedberg (Chemistry; invented the ultracentrifuge) for studying them, and Jean Perrin (Physics) partly for experiments on how their particles settle
Albert Einstein explained Brownian motion in 1905 as the result of collisions with moving molecules
Butter holds water droplets in fat, while milk holds fat droplets in water; both are emulsions
Adding salt can make the particles clump together, called coagulation or flocculation
Electrostatic precipitators clean smoke from factory chimneys by charging its tiny particles and collecting them on metal plates
Alum clumps dirt particles in water treatment; river clay clumping in salty seawater helps form deltas
Their particles usually carry the same kind of charge, so they repel each other; in an electric field they drift toward an electrode (electrophoresis)
Lyophilic types have particles that attract the surrounding liquid; lyophobic types do not
Above a certain concentration, soap molecules form micelles, making “association” types
Thixotropic ones get runnier when shaken or stirred and thicken again at rest
Gold and silver particles make the Roman Lycurgus Cup look green or red; Michael Faraday made a ruby-red gold sample in 1857
NASA’s Stardust probe caught comet dust in aerogel, a super-light solid made by drying a gel

trap.title: Not solution or suspension
trap.body: These mixtures are defined by particle size, so tossups about them often describe solutions and suspensions too. In a solution, like salt water, the particles are single molecules or ions and a light beam passes through unseen; in a suspension, like muddy water, the particles are big enough to settle out or be filtered. Players also blurt one type, like “emulsion” or “aerosol,” when the question wants the whole family.
trap.fix: Settles out or filters out means suspension; perfectly clear with no visible beam means solution; scatters a beam (the Tyndall effect) but never settles means this answer. Listen for “these mixtures” and give the general name unless the question clearly asks for one type.
trap.line: Real answer line: Colloids (accept colloidal dispersions or colloidal suspensions; prompt on heterogeneous mixtures or dispersions; do not accept “suspension” or “solution” alone)

topics.name: Sulfur
topics.kicker: Element 16 · The yellow “brimstone” of volcanoes and gunpowder
topics.dates: Known since ancient times; Lavoisier argued it was an element, 1777
topics.briefing: Sulfur is the bright yellow element that crusts the rocks around volcanoes and hot springs; its old name, “brimstone,” means “burning stone,” and it really does burn, with an eerie blue flame. The rotten-egg smell people blame on it comes from hydrogen sulfide; pure sulfur has almost no smell. It goes into gunpowder, toughens rubber in Charles Goodyear’s vulcanization process, and is the key ingredient in sulfuric acid, a workhorse of the chemical industry.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Herman Frasch invented a way to mine this element from deep deposits in Louisiana and Texas by pumping superheated water down to melt it and then blowing the liquid to the surface with compressed air. Refineries also recover large amounts of this element from oil and natural gas.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this yellow element with atomic number 16, which burns with a blue flame.

tossups.p: When molten samples of this element are heated past about 160 degrees Celsius, they suddenly become much thicker, because its eight-atom rings break open and link into long chains. Pouring that hot liquid into cold water makes a rubbery “plastic” form of this element.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this yellow nonmetal, element 16, which sits just below oxygen on the periodic table.

tossups.p: The rhombic form of this element changes into a needle-shaped monoclinic form when it is heated above about 95 degrees Celsius. Both of those forms are built from crown-shaped rings of eight atoms of this element.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this element, which lies just below oxygen in group 16 and forms yellow crystals near volcanoes.

tossups.p: Charles Goodyear found in 1839 that heating natural rubber with this element made the rubber tough and far less sticky, because atoms of this element form cross-links between the rubber’s long chains. That process, vulcanization, is named for the Roman god of fire.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this element, a yellow nonmetal with atomic number 16 that burns with a blue flame.

tossups.p: Paracelsus [“par-uh-SELL-sus”] taught that all matter was made of three principles: salt, mercury, and this element. Black gunpowder is a mixture of saltpeter, charcoal, and this element, which makes up about a tenth of it.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this yellow element, which burns with a blue flame to make a choking gas called its dioxide.

tossups.p: Cornelis van Niel [“van NEEL”] studied purple bacteria that use a compound of hydrogen and this element instead of water in photosynthesis, giving off this element instead of oxygen. That work helped show that the oxygen plants release comes from water.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this element, whose compound with hydrogen smells like rotten eggs.

tossups.p: Volcanoes on Jupiter’s moon Io spray out this element and its oxides, coloring the moon yellow and orange. The thick clouds of Venus are made of droplets of a strong acid built from hydrogen, oxygen, and this element.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this element, number 16 on the periodic table, which forms yellow crystals around volcanic vents.

tossups.p: Gerhard Domagk [“DOH-mahk”] won the 1939 Nobel Prize in medicine for discovering Prontosil, the first of a family of germ-fighting drugs named for this element. Bridges between atoms of this element in the amino acid cysteine help hold proteins like keratin in shape.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this yellow element that lies below oxygen in group 16.

tossups.p: Compounds of this element called thiols give skunk spray its stink and are added to natural gas so that leaks can be smelled. Other compounds of this element make your eyes water when you cut onions.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this element, whose compound with hydrogen is the source of the smell of rotten eggs.

tossups.p: In the contact process, a vanadium oxide catalyst helps turn the dioxide of this element into its trioxide, a key step in making one of the most-produced industrial chemicals, a strong acid. Burning coal that contains this element releases a gas that helps cause acid rain.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this yellow element with atomic number 16, whose compound with hydrogen smells like rotten eggs.

tossups.p: This element forms a hexafluoride that insulates high-voltage electrical equipment and has an octahedral shape, an example of an “expanded octet.” Like oxygen just above it, this element has six valence electrons.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this yellow nonmetal, which crusts the rocks around volcanic vents and hot springs and burns with a blue flame.

tossups.p: In 1777, Antoine Lavoisier [“lah-vwah-ZYAY”] helped convince other scientists that this substance was an element, not a compound. Its old English name, found in the King James Bible, means “burning stone.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this yellow element, which burns with a blue flame and sits below oxygen on the periodic table.

tossups.p: At the Kawah Ijen [“KAH-wah EE-jen”] volcano in Indonesia, gases rich in this element burn with blue flames at night, and miners carry chunks of its yellow solid down the mountain. Bacteria at deep-sea hydrothermal vents make food using energy from its compounds.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this element with atomic number 16, whose yellow crystals form around volcanic vents.

tossups.p: In chemical names, the prefix “thio-,” as in the photographers’ fixing chemical nicknamed “hypo,” means an atom of this element has taken the place of an oxygen atom. Epsom salt and gypsum both contain an ion made of this element and four oxygen atoms.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this element, which forms yellow crystals and has atomic number 16.

tossups.p: Pyrite, or “fool’s gold,” is a compound of iron and this element, and galena, the main ore of lead, combines lead with it. Cinnabar, the bright red ore of mercury, is a compound of mercury and this element.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this yellow element, whose compound with hydrogen gives rotten eggs their smell.

clues.t: Element 16, a yellow, brittle nonmetal
Its compound with hydrogen smells like rotten eggs; the pure element has almost no smell
Its old English name, found in the King James Bible, means “burning stone”
Sits just below oxygen in group 16, the chalcogens; like oxygen, it has six valence electrons
Burns with a blue flame, making a choking gas, its dioxide
Forms yellow crystals around volcanoes, hot springs, and volcanic vents
Black gunpowder is saltpeter (potassium nitrate), charcoal, and this element
Charles Goodyear’s vulcanization (1839): heating rubber with it makes cross-links that keep rubber tough and not sticky
Key ingredient of one of the most-produced industrial chemicals, a strong acid made by the contact process
Burning coal that contains it releases a gas that helps cause acid rain
Its molecules are crown-shaped rings of eight atoms
Volcanoes on Jupiter’s moon Io spray it out; the clouds of Venus are droplets of an acid made with it
Found in the amino acids cysteine and methionine; bridges between cysteines hold proteins like keratin in shape
Thiols containing it give skunk spray its stink and are added to natural gas; other compounds of it make cut onions sting your eyes
Pyrite (“fool’s gold”) combines it with iron, galena with lead, and cinnabar with mercury
Herman Frasch’s process melts underground deposits with superheated water and blows the liquid up with compressed air; refineries also recover it from oil and gas
Molten samples heated past about 160 °C suddenly thicken, as the rings break open into long chains
Pouring the hot liquid into cold water makes a rubbery “plastic” form
Its rhombic form, stable at room temperature, turns into a needle-shaped monoclinic form above about 95 °C
Paracelsus’s three principles of matter: salt, mercury, and this element
Antoine Lavoisier helped convince scientists in 1777 that it is an element, not a compound
Purple bacteria use its hydrogen compound instead of water in photosynthesis; Cornelis van Niel used them to argue that plants’ oxygen comes from water
Bacteria at deep-sea hydrothermal vents get energy from its compounds, a process called chemosynthesis
Gerhard Domagk won the 1939 Nobel Prize for Prontosil, the first of the germ-fighting drugs named for it
Its octahedral hexafluoride, an “expanded octet” molecule, insulates high-voltage equipment
The prefix “thio-” in a chemical name means it has replaced an oxygen atom, as in the photographers’ fixer “hypo”
Epsom salt and gypsum contain an ion made of it and four oxygen atoms
At Kawah Ijen volcano in Indonesia, gases rich in it burn with blue flames at night

trap.title: Element, not its compounds
trap.body: Tossups on this element are full of its famous compounds: the rotten-egg gas it makes with hydrogen, the strong acid made by the contact process, the dioxide behind acid rain, and minerals like pyrite and gypsum. Answering with a compound, like “hydrogen sulfide” or “sulfuric acid,” is wrong when the question asks for the element. Its group 16 neighbors, oxygen above and selenium below, are the other traps.
trap.fix: If the question says “this element,” give the element: either spelling, sulfur or sulphur, or its symbol, S. Save compound names for questions that say “this compound,” “this gas,” or “this acid.”

topics.name: Chromatography
topics.kicker: Separating a mixture by how fast its parts travel · From ink to crime labs
topics.briefing: Chromatography separates a mixture by letting its parts race through a material at different speeds: put a dot of black marker on paper, dip the edge in water, and the dot can split into bands of blue, pink, and yellow as the water climbs. Russian-Italian botanist Mikhail Tsvet used a tube packed with chalk to separate the colored pigments in leaves, and he named the method “color writing.” Crime labs use it to identify inks, drugs, and other evidence.
topics.answerHtml: Chromatography (accept specific types like paper chromatography, gas chromatography, or thin-layer chromatography; do not accept “electrophoresis”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Mikhail Tsvet [“TSVET”], whose last name means “color” in Russian, named this technique after he separated the pigments in plant leaves by pouring their extract through a glass column packed with chalk. Its name comes from Greek words for “color writing.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this technique for separating mixtures, which comes in paper, column, and gas types.

tossups.p: Archer Martin and Richard Synge [“SING”] shared the 1952 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for inventing the partition type of this technique, which they used to separate amino acids. Martin also helped develop a form of this technique that carries samples through a column with an inert gas.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this lab technique that separates a mixture as a mobile phase carries it past a stationary phase.

tossups.p: The efficiency of a column used in this technique is often measured by counting “theoretical plates,” an idea borrowed from distillation. In the classic leaf-pigment version of this technique, orange carotene usually travels farthest, while chlorophyll b lags behind the other pigments.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this separation technique, whose paper version can split black ink into several colors.

tossups.p: In the paper and thin-layer versions of this technique, a spot’s Rf value equals the distance it moved divided by the distance the solvent front moved, so the value always falls between 0 and 1. The starting line is drawn in pencil, because ink would dissolve and run.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this technique that separates the dyes in markers as a solvent climbs up a strip of paper.

tossups.p: In the size-exclusion type of this technique, the largest molecules come out of the column first, because they are too big to wander into the tiny pores of the beads inside. The affinity type uses molecules that bind tightly to just one target, like an antibody grabbing its antigen.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this family of techniques that separate mixtures using a mobile phase and a stationary phase.

tossups.p: Labs that test athletes for banned drugs often pair the gas form of this technique with mass spectrometry. In that gas form, a carrier gas such as helium sweeps vaporized samples through a long, thin, coiled column inside an oven.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this separation technique, whose paper form makes ink spots spread out into bands of color.

tossups.p: In the reverse-phase type of this technique, a nonpolar stationary phase holds back nonpolar molecules while a polar solvent rushes polar ones through. A high-performance liquid version of this technique uses pumps to push solvent through a column of tiny particles at high pressure.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this technique that separates the parts of a mixture by how fast they travel past a stationary phase.

tossups.p: Chemists often check the results of the thin-layer form of this technique under ultraviolet light or in a jar of iodine vapor, which turns the separated spots brown. Spraying the paper form with ninhydrin [“nin-HY-drin”] makes amino acids show up as purple spots.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this technique, used in classroom labs to separate the pigments in leaves.

tossups.p: In the column form of this technique, the solvent poured in at the top is called the eluent [“ELL-yoo-ent”], and the liquid that drips out the bottom carrying separated compounds is the eluate. Each compound comes out at a different time, depending on how strongly it sticks to the packing.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this technique, whose paper form can separate the green and yellow pigments in spinach leaves.

tossups.p: The ion-exchange type of this technique separates molecules by electric charge, using a resin with charged groups on its surface. The chiral type of this technique can separate the two mirror-image forms of a drug molecule.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this technique, whose gas, paper, and thin-layer forms all separate mixtures by how fast their parts move.

tossups.p: In the gas form of this technique, each compound is identified by its retention time, how long it takes to reach the detector, and the results appear as a graph of peaks. A common detector for that gas form, the flame ionization detector, burns the compounds in a hydrogen flame.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this technique for separating the parts of a mixture, whose paper form can split marker ink into colors.

tossups.p: Forensic scientists use this technique to compare the ink on a forged document with the ink in a suspect’s pen, and to find traces of gasoline in the debris of a fire. Its paper form works because different dyes cling to the paper with different strengths.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this technique that separates the parts of a mixture as a solvent carries them along.

tossups.p: In a two-dimensional form of this technique, a sheet of paper is run in one direction, turned 90 degrees, and run again with a different solvent, a method once used to separate the amino acids that make up proteins. Supercritical carbon dioxide can serve as the moving phase in another form of this technique.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this technique for separating mixtures, whose name comes from the Greek for “color writing.”

tossups.p: Molecules that cling strongly to the stationary phase move slowly in this technique, while those that dissolve well in the mobile phase race ahead. In its thin-layer form, the stationary phase is usually a coating of silica gel on a flat plate.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this technique, used to split marker ink into separate colors on a strip of paper.

tossups.p: In the paper form of this technique, chemists often describe the stationary phase as a thin layer of water held by the paper’s cellulose fibers. Mikhail Tsvet [“TSVET”] invented this technique in the early 1900s while studying plant pigments.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this technique that separates a mixture as a mobile phase carries its parts along at different speeds.

clues.t: A technique that separates the parts of a mixture because they travel at different speeds
A mobile phase (a liquid or gas) carries the mixture past a stationary phase
Its paper version splits black marker ink into bands of color as water climbs the paper
Comes in paper, thin-layer, column, gas, and liquid types
Its name comes from Greek words meaning “color writing”
Invented by Mikhail Tsvet (whose name means “color” in Russian), who separated leaf pigments in a column of chalk and named it in 1906
Rf value = distance a spot moved ÷ distance the solvent front moved, always between 0 and 1
In the paper form, the solvent rises up the paper by capillary action
The starting line is drawn in pencil, because ink would dissolve and run
Classroom labs use it to separate chlorophyll a, chlorophyll b, and carotene from spinach leaves
Gas form: a carrier gas like helium sweeps vaporized samples through a long coiled column in an oven
Its gas form is often paired with mass spectrometry, as in drug tests for athletes
Forensic labs use it to compare inks and to find traces of gasoline in fire debris
Thin-layer form: a plate coated with silica gel is the stationary phase
Archer Martin and Richard Synge won the 1952 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for inventing its partition type
In the classic leaf-pigment lab, orange carotene usually travels farthest, while chlorophyll b lags behind the other pigments
Column efficiency is counted in “theoretical plates,” an idea borrowed from distillation
Size-exclusion type: the largest molecules come out first, since they can’t enter the beads’ tiny pores
Affinity type: uses a molecule that binds just one target, like an antibody grabbing its antigen
Ion-exchange type separates molecules by charge with a charged resin; chiral type separates mirror-image forms
Reverse-phase type: a nonpolar stationary phase with a polar solvent
High-performance liquid form: pumps push solvent through a column of tiny particles at high pressure
The eluent is the solvent that goes in; the eluate, carrying separated compounds, comes out
Gas form: compounds are identified by retention time, often with a flame ionization detector that burns them in a hydrogen flame
Spots show up under ultraviolet light or in iodine vapor; ninhydrin turns amino acids purple
Two-dimensional paper form: run once, turned 90 degrees, and run again with a new solvent
Supercritical carbon dioxide can serve as the mobile phase
In the paper form, the stationary phase is often described as water held by the paper’s cellulose fibers

trap.title: Not electrophoresis or distillation
trap.body: Other lab techniques also pull mixtures apart. Distillation separates liquids by boiling them off at different temperatures, and electrophoresis uses an electric field to drag charged molecules like DNA through a gel. Mass spectrometry sorts charged fragments by mass to identify a substance, and because it is so often paired with this technique, players sometimes buzz with the wrong half.
trap.fix: Mobile phase, stationary phase, Rf values, solvent fronts, retention times, and Tsvet mean this technique. An electric current pulling DNA through a gel means electrophoresis; boiling and condensing means distillation.
trap.line: Real answer line: Chromatography (accept specific types like paper chromatography, gas chromatography, or thin-layer chromatography; do not accept “electrophoresis”)

topics.name: Hydrogen bonds
topics.kicker: Hydrogen’s pull on a nearby N, O, or F atom · Holds water and DNA together
topics.briefing: A hydrogen bond is an attraction between a hydrogen atom attached to nitrogen, oxygen, or fluorine and a lone pair of electrons on another such atom nearby. Each one is much weaker than the covalent bonds inside a molecule, but together they work wonders: they give water its unusually high boiling point, let ice float, hold the two strands of DNA together, and help fold proteins into their shapes.
topics.answerHtml: Hydrogen bonds (accept hydrogen bonding or H-bonds; prompt on intermolecular forces or dipole-dipole interactions; do not accept “hydrogen” alone)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In 1920, Wendell Latimer and Worth Rodebush used these attractions to explain why water behaves so strangely for such a small molecule. Linus Pauling’s book _The Nature of the Chemical Bond_ made these attractions famous, and he later used them to propose the alpha helix and beta sheet in proteins.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these attractions between a hydrogen atom on one molecule and a nitrogen, oxygen, or fluorine atom on another.

tossups.p: The strongest known example of these attractions is found in the bifluoride ion, in which one hydrogen atom sits between two fluorine atoms. Partly because of these attractions, hydrogen fluoride boils at about 20 degrees Celsius, while hydrogen chloride boils far below zero.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these attractions, which form when hydrogen is bonded to nitrogen, oxygen, or fluorine.

tossups.p: Ethanol boils at about 78 degrees Celsius but dimethyl ether, which has the same chemical formula, boils below zero, because only ethanol molecules can form these attractions with each other. These attractions are usually drawn as dashed or dotted lines between molecules.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these intermolecular attractions, which give water its unusually high boiling point.

tossups.p: Ortho-nitrophenol boils at a lower temperature than para-nitrophenol because each of its molecules forms one of these attractions within itself instead of with its neighbors. In infrared spectra, these attractions make the peak for an O–H group broad and smeared out.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these attractions that hold together the two strands of DNA.

tossups.p: Guanine and cytosine share three of these attractions, while adenine and thymine share only two, so DNA rich in guanine and cytosine is harder to pull apart. The enzyme helicase breaks these attractions to unzip DNA before it is copied.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these attractions between a hydrogen atom and a nearby nitrogen, oxygen, or fluorine atom.

tossups.p: Stephanie Kwolek’s Kevlar fibers are strong partly because these attractions link neighboring polymer chains into sheets. Chains of nylon also cling to each other through these attractions between their amide groups.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these attractions, often drawn as dotted lines, that also make water molecules stick to each other.

tossups.p: In an alpha helix, these attractions form between the C=O group of one amino acid and the N–H group of the amino acid four positions farther along the chain. Beta pleated sheets are held together by these attractions between side-by-side strands.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these attractions, which also hold the base pairs of DNA together.

tossups.p: Ammonia boils at a much higher temperature than phosphine, its heavier cousin, because ammonia molecules can form these attractions. Each water molecule can form up to four of these attractions, which lock ice into an open, six-sided pattern.
tossups.r: That open pattern makes ice float. For 10 points, name these attractions between water molecules.

tossups.p: Acetic acid molecules pair up into dimers, even as a vapor, through two of these attractions between their acid groups. In each of these attractions, the atom attached to the hydrogen is called the donor, and the atom offering a lone pair is called the acceptor.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these attractions, usually the strongest of the three main intermolecular forces.

tossups.p: Water boils at 100 degrees Celsius, but hydrogen sulfide, a heavier molecule with the same bent shape, boils at about negative 60 degrees, because its molecules form almost none of these attractions. These attractions also give water its high surface tension.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these attractions between molecules, which form when hydrogen is attached to nitrogen, oxygen, or fluorine.

tossups.p: The long cellulose chains in cotton and wood cling to each other through many of these attractions, and water gets in between them, which is one reason wet paper tears so easily. Heating a protein, as when you cook an egg, breaks these attractions and unravels its shape.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these attractions, often drawn as dotted lines, that link water molecules to each other.

tossups.p: These attractions are much weaker than covalent bonds but stronger than the London dispersion forces between molecules of similar size. Some chemists describe them as an especially strong type of dipole–dipole attraction.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these attractions involving a hydrogen atom bonded to a nitrogen, oxygen, or fluorine atom, which hold DNA’s two strands together.

tossups.p: Water’s high heat of vaporization, which lets sweat cool the body, comes from the energy needed to break these attractions. Cohesion from these attractions helps water climb up the thin xylem tubes of tall trees and lets water striders walk on a pond.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these attractions that make water molecules stick together, giving water its high boiling point.

tossups.p: In 1953, James Watson worked out how DNA bases pair up through these attractions by shuffling cardboard cutouts of the bases on his desk. These attractions between matching bases, along with the stacking of the bases, hold the double helix together.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these weak attractions, two of which link adenine to thymine.

tossups.p: On a graph of boiling points for the hydrogen compounds of groups 15, 16, and 17, the lightest member of each group sticks out far above the trend because of these attractions. Those three standouts are ammonia, water, and hydrogen fluoride.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these intermolecular attractions, which also hold proteins and DNA in shape.

Make water molecules stick together, giving water its high boiling point and letting ice float
Hold the two strands of DNA together between paired bases
Usually drawn as dashed or dotted lines between molecules
Usually the strongest of the three main intermolecular forces, but much weaker than a covalent bond
Guanine–cytosine pairs share three; adenine–thymine pairs share two
The enzyme helicase breaks them to unzip DNA before it is copied
Each water molecule can form up to four, locking ice into an open, six-sided pattern
Water boils at 100 °C, but heavier hydrogen sulfide, which forms almost none, boils at about −60 °C
Cause water’s cohesion and high surface tension, which help water climb tree xylem and let water striders walk
Water’s high specific heat and heat of vaporization come from the energy needed to break them
Hold proteins’ alpha helices and beta pleated sheets in shape
Heating a protein, as when you cook an egg, breaks them and unravels its shape
The atom attached to the hydrogen is the donor; the atom offering a lone pair is the acceptor
Often described as an especially strong type of dipole–dipole attraction
In 1920, Wendell Latimer and Worth Rodebush used them to explain water’s strange behavior
Linus Pauling made them famous in _The Nature of the Chemical Bond_ and used them to propose the alpha helix
Hydrogen fluoride boils near 20 °C, far above hydrogen chloride; the bifluoride ion has the strongest known one
Ethanol (boils near 78 °C) forms them, but dimethyl ether, with the same formula, boils below zero
Ortho-nitrophenol forms one within each molecule, so it boils lower than para-nitrophenol
In infrared spectra, they make the O–H peak broad and smeared out
In an alpha helix, each C=O group pairs with the N–H group of the amino acid four positions along
Link the chains of Stephanie Kwolek’s Kevlar into strong sheets; also join nylon’s amide groups
Acetic acid molecules pair into dimers, even as a vapor, through two of them
Ammonia boils far higher than heavier phosphine because ammonia molecules form them
On a graph of boiling points of the group 15–17 hydrogen compounds, ammonia, water, and hydrogen fluoride stick out above the trend
Join the cellulose chains in cotton and wood; water gets between them, so wet paper tears easily
In 1953, James Watson worked out base pairing by shuffling cardboard cutouts of the bases

trap.title: Between molecules, not inside
trap.body: These attractions are easy to confuse with the covalent bonds inside a molecule: in water, the O–H bonds holding each molecule together are covalent, while these attractions link one water molecule to the next. Players also blurt “hydrogen,” the element, or give the broad category “intermolecular forces,” which only earns a prompt. London dispersion forces and dipole–dipole forces are other intermolecular forces with their own answer lines.
trap.fix: Hydrogen attached to nitrogen, oxygen, or fluorine pulling on a neighbor, DNA base pairs, or water’s high boiling point mean this answer, so give its full name, not just “hydrogen.” Electrons shared inside a molecule mean covalent bonds; temporary dipoles in any molecule mean London dispersion forces.
trap.line: Real answer line: Hydrogen bonds (accept hydrogen bonding or H-bonds; prompt on intermolecular forces or dipole-dipole interactions; do not accept “hydrogen” alone)

topics.name: Alcohols (chemistry)
topics.kicker: Organic compounds with an –OH group · Their names end in “-ol”
topics.briefing: In chemistry, an alcohol is any organic compound with a hydroxyl group, an oxygen-hydrogen pair written –OH, attached to a carbon atom. Their names end in “-ol”: methanol has long been used as a race-car fuel, isopropanol is the rubbing alcohol in first-aid kits, and ethylene glycol keeps car engines from freezing. Because that –OH group forms hydrogen bonds, alcohols boil at much higher temperatures than hydrocarbons of similar size.
topics.answerHtml: Alcohols (accept alkanols; prompt on hydroxyl compounds; do not accept “hydroxyl” alone or specific alcohols like “ethanol”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Herbert C. Brown shared the 1979 Nobel Prize in Chemistry partly for hydroboration, a two-step reaction that turns alkenes into these compounds, putting the oxygen-containing group on the less crowded carbon. These compounds also form when sodium borohydride reduces an aldehyde or a ketone.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these organic compounds that contain a hydroxyl group and have names ending in “-ol.”

tossups.p: The Lucas test uses zinc chloride in hydrochloric acid to tell three kinds of these compounds apart: tertiary ones turn the mixture cloudy almost at once, secondary ones take a few minutes, and primary ones barely react.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this class of organic compounds, which includes methanol and ethanol.

tossups.p: Orange potassium dichromate turns green as it oxidizes primary members of this class into aldehydes and then into carboxylic acids, while secondary members become ketones. Tertiary members of this class resist that oxidation.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this class of compounds with an –OH group, such as isopropanol and ethanol.

tossups.p: Dropping sodium metal into these compounds releases hydrogen gas and forms alkoxides, which react with alkyl halides to make ethers in Alexander Williamson’s ether synthesis. These compounds are only about as acidic as water.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this class of compounds that includes methanol, whose names end in “-ol.”

tossups.p: Victor Grignard [“green-YAR”] won the 1912 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for reagents that add to ketones to form tertiary members of this class. Lithium aluminum hydride can also produce these compounds from esters or carboxylic acids.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these organic compounds containing a hydroxyl group, such as ethanol and isopropanol.

tossups.p: Heating these compounds with concentrated sulfuric acid can strip out a water molecule to form an alkene or, at a lower temperature, join two of their molecules into an ether. Industrial chemists make one of these compounds by reacting ethene with steam over a phosphoric acid catalyst.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this class of organic compounds, whose simplest member is methanol and whose names end in “-ol.”

tossups.p: In Fischer esterification, an acid catalyst helps one of these compounds react with a carboxylic acid to form a fruity-smelling ester and water. Glycerol, a member of this class with three –OH groups, forms the backbone of fats.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these compounds, such as ethanol and methanol, whose names end in “-ol.”

tossups.p: This class’s name comes from the Arabic word for kohl, a fine black powder used as eye makeup. Menthol from mint leaves, cholesterol, and retinol, also called vitamin A, all belong to this class.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this class of organic compounds with a hydroxyl group, whose names end in “-ol.”

tossups.p: Octanol, a member of this class with a long carbon chain, barely dissolves in water, so chemists shake drugs with octanol and water to measure whether they prefer oily or watery surroundings. The smallest members of this class, such as methanol and ethanol, mix completely with water.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this class of organic compounds that contain an –OH group and have names ending in “-ol.”

tossups.p: Members of this class are called primary, secondary, or tertiary depending on how many carbon atoms are attached to the carbon holding their –OH group. The tertiary example called tert-butanol has three methyl groups on that carbon.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this class of compounds that includes isopropanol, the antiseptic liquid found in many first-aid kits.

tossups.p: Antifreeze is mostly ethylene glycol, a member of this class with two –OH groups, which makes it a diol. Sugar-free gums are often sweetened with xylitol and sorbitol, which also belong to this class.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this class of organic compounds whose names usually end in “-ol,” such as methanol.

tossups.p: Methanol, the simplest member of this class, was once made by heating wood without air and was later made mostly from carbon monoxide and hydrogen gas. Methanol is highly toxic, and it has long been used as a fuel for race cars.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this class of organic compounds, which also includes ethanol and isopropanol.

tossups.p: Yeast turn sugar into carbon dioxide and one of these compounds during fermentation. Brazil fuels many of its cars with that compound made from sugarcane, and most American gasoline contains about 10 percent of it.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this class of organic compounds, which have a hydroxyl group and names ending in “-ol.”

tossups.p: Thiols, sometimes called mercaptans, are the sulfur versions of these compounds, with an –SH group in place of their –OH group. In infrared spectra, these compounds show a broad peak caused by their O–H bonds.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this class of compounds, including ethanol and methanol, whose names end in “-ol.”

tossups.p: Phenols have an –OH group attached directly to a benzene ring and are much more acidic, so they are usually counted as a separate class from these compounds. Because they form hydrogen bonds, these compounds boil at higher temperatures than alkanes of similar size.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these organic compounds, such as isopropanol, that contain a hydroxyl group.

Their names end in the suffix “-ol”
Include methanol, ethanol, and isopropanol
