trap.title: The class, not one member
trap.body: Tossups on this class lean on famous members like ethanol, methanol, and isopropanol, so players blurt one compound’s name, which is wrong when the question asks for the whole class. Others answer “hydroxyl,” the name of the –OH group itself, rather than the compounds that contain it. Phenols also carry –OH groups but are a separate class, and carboxylic acids hide an –OH inside their –COOH group.
trap.fix: Listen for “these compounds” or “this class,” and give the family name. If the question asks for the –OH group itself, say “hydroxyl”; an –OH on a benzene ring means phenol; an –OH next to a C=O in a –COOH group means carboxylic acid.
trap.line: Real answer line: Alcohols (accept alkanols; prompt on hydroxyl compounds; do not accept “hydroxyl” alone or specific alcohols like “ethanol”)

topics.name: Gibbs free energy
topics.kicker: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS · Its sign tells whether a reaction can happen on its own
topics.dates: Introduced by J. Willard Gibbs in the 1870s
topics.briefing: Gibbs free energy, written G, tells chemists whether a reaction can happen on its own. Its change, ΔG, combines two things nature favors, giving off heat (a negative ΔH) and spreading out energy and matter (a positive ΔS), in the equation ΔG = ΔH − TΔS; when ΔG is negative, the reaction is spontaneous, though it may still be very slow. It is named for Josiah Willard Gibbs, who earned the first American doctorate in engineering, at Yale.
topics.answerHtml: Gibbs free energy (or Gibbs energy or G; accept delta G; prompt on free energy or Gibbs; do not accept “Helmholtz free energy”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: This quantity was described in “On the Equilibrium of Heterogeneous Substances,” a long paper published in parts in the 1870s by a Yale professor. That paper also defined the chemical potential, the change in this quantity for each mole of a substance added to a mixture.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity, equal to enthalpy minus temperature times entropy, whose change is negative for spontaneous reactions.

tossups.p: The standard change in this quantity equals negative RT times the natural log of the equilibrium constant, so a negative value means products are favored at equilibrium. Photosynthesis has a large positive change in this quantity, so plants can carry it out only by capturing energy from sunlight.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity whose change is negative for any spontaneous process at constant temperature and pressure.

tossups.p: The standard change in this quantity for a battery’s reaction equals negative n times the Faraday constant times the cell’s standard voltage, so a positive voltage means a negative change in this quantity. Combining that relationship with the reaction quotient gives the Nernst equation.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this thermodynamic quantity, which combines enthalpy and entropy to predict whether a reaction is spontaneous.

tossups.p: An equation named for this quantity’s namesake and Hermann von Helmholtz describes how this quantity changes with temperature. At constant temperature and pressure, a system settles into the state where this quantity is as low as possible.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity, whose change is zero for a system at equilibrium and negative for spontaneous reactions.

tossups.p: Cells drive uphill reactions by coupling them to the breakdown of ATP, which changes this quantity by about negative 30 kilojoules per mole under standard conditions. Reactions that lower this quantity are called exergonic, while reactions that raise it are called endergonic.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this thermodynamic quantity, whose change is negative for spontaneous reactions.

tossups.p: The change in this quantity favors diamond slowly turning into graphite at room temperature, but that change happens far too slowly to notice, showing that a negative value of this quantity’s change says nothing about how fast a reaction goes.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity, whose change equals the change in enthalpy minus temperature times the change in entropy.

tossups.p: A reaction that releases heat and increases entropy has a negative change in this quantity at every temperature, while one that absorbs heat and decreases entropy never does. Ice melts above 0 degrees Celsius because the entropy term wins out in the change in this quantity.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity, defined as enthalpy minus temperature times entropy, whose change is negative for spontaneous reactions.

tossups.p: At constant temperature and pressure, the change in this quantity gives the maximum amount of useful work, not counting work done pushing back the atmosphere, that a process can do. Its Helmholtz counterpart is used at constant volume instead.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity, whose change is negative for spontaneous reactions and is named for a Yale scientist.

tossups.p: The change in this quantity equals its standard change plus RT times the natural log of the reaction quotient, Q. When this quantity’s change reaches zero, the reaction quotient equals the equilibrium constant, and the reaction has reached equilibrium.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity, whose change is negative for spontaneous processes at constant temperature and pressure.

tossups.p: A liquid’s normal boiling point is the temperature at which the change in this quantity for vaporizing is zero, so it equals the enthalpy of vaporization divided by the entropy of vaporization. Above that temperature, boiling happens on its own.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity, which equals enthalpy minus temperature times entropy.

tossups.p: A protein folds up on its own because folding lowers this quantity, even though the folded chain is more orderly, partly because the water molecules around the protein gain entropy. Protein unfolding raises this quantity at body temperature.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity, whose negative change marks a spontaneous process.

tossups.p: This quantity is named for the scientist who earned the first doctorate in engineering granted in the United States and who also wrote the phase rule, F = C − P + 2, which counts how many variables in a system can change freely.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity, named for that Yale scientist, whose negative change marks a spontaneous reaction at constant temperature and pressure.

tossups.p: Elements in their standard states, such as oxygen gas, have a standard change of formation of zero for this quantity. Subtracting the reactants’ standard formation values from the products’ values gives the standard change in this quantity for a reaction.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity, whose change is negative for reactions that can happen on their own.

tossups.p: Limestone breaks down into lime and carbon dioxide only when it is heated strongly in a kiln, because only at high temperatures does the entropy term make this quantity’s change negative. Endothermic reactions that increase entropy become spontaneous only above a certain temperature.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity whose sign tells whether a reaction can happen on its own at a given temperature.

tossups.p: Dissolving ammonium nitrate in water absorbs heat, yet it happens on its own because the rise in entropy makes the change in this quantity negative. That is why instant cold packs work.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this thermodynamic quantity, whose change equals the change in enthalpy minus temperature times the change in entropy.

clues.t: A negative change means a reaction is spontaneous (it can happen on its own); a positive change means it is not
Its change equals the change in enthalpy minus temperature times the change in entropy
Named for a Yale professor who earned the first American doctorate in engineering
Its change is zero for a system at equilibrium
Usually measured in kilojoules per mole; its change is written with a capital delta (Δ)
Exergonic reactions lower it; endergonic reactions raise it
Releasing heat plus increasing entropy: spontaneous at all temperatures; absorbing heat plus decreasing entropy: never
Endothermic reactions that increase entropy, like limestone breaking down in a kiln, are spontaneous only at high temperatures
Ice melts on its own above 0 °C because the entropy term wins out
Used at constant temperature and pressure; its Helmholtz counterpart is used at constant volume
A negative change says nothing about speed: diamond turning into graphite is favored but far too slow to notice
Cells couple uphill reactions to ATP breakdown, which changes it by about −30 kilojoules per mole
Dissolving ammonium nitrate absorbs heat but is still spontaneous, because entropy rises enough
Its standard change of formation is zero for elements in their standard states
Its standard change equals −RT ln K, so a negative value means the equilibrium constant K is greater than 1
Its change equals its standard change plus RT ln Q, where Q is the reaction quotient
Its standard change equals −n × the Faraday constant × the standard cell voltage; combining this with Q gives the Nernst equation
An equation named for its namesake and Hermann von Helmholtz describes how it changes with temperature
At constant temperature and pressure, a system settles into the state where it is as low as possible
The chemical potential is its change for each mole of a substance added to a mixture
Described in “On the Equilibrium of Heterogeneous Substances,” published in parts in the 1870s
Its namesake also wrote the phase rule, F = C − P + 2
Its change gives the maximum useful work (not counting pushing back the atmosphere) a process can do
Photosynthesis has a large positive change, so plants can carry it out only by capturing energy from sunlight
Its change for vaporizing is zero at the normal boiling point, so that temperature = enthalpy ÷ entropy of vaporization
Protein folding lowers it even though the chain gets more orderly, partly because the surrounding water gains entropy

trap.title: Not enthalpy, not Helmholtz
trap.body: This quantity is built from enthalpy and entropy, so its tossups are full of clues about heat and disorder that tempt players to buzz with one of those two. Its cousin, the Helmholtz free energy, is used at constant volume instead of constant pressure and has a different answer line. Saying just “free energy” or “Gibbs” only earns a prompt.
trap.fix: If the clue asks whether a reaction is spontaneous, or links equilibrium constants, cell voltage, or ATP coupling, give the full name with “Gibbs.” Heat released or absorbed means enthalpy; disorder means entropy; constant volume means Helmholtz.
trap.line: Real answer line: Gibbs free energy (or Gibbs energy or G; accept delta G; prompt on free energy or Gibbs; do not accept “Helmholtz free energy”)

topics.name: Benzene
topics.kicker: A flat ring of six carbon atoms · The model aromatic compound
topics.briefing: Benzene is a flat ring of six carbon atoms, each holding one hydrogen, with the formula C₆H₆. Michael Faraday discovered it in 1825, but its structure puzzled chemists until August Kekulé proposed a hexagon in 1865, later saying the idea came to him in a dream of a snake biting its own tail. Six electrons shared around the whole ring make it unusually stable, the classic example of an “aromatic” compound.
topics.answerHtml: Benzene (or C6H6; accept benzol; prompt on aromatic hydrocarbon or arene; do not accept “toluene” or other benzene derivatives)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Vanillin, which gives vanilla its flavor, and cinnamaldehyde [“sin-uh-MAL-duh-hyde”], which flavors cinnamon, are built on this compound’s ring; pleasant smells like theirs are why chemists first called its family of compounds “aromatic.” August Kekulé [“KAY-kuh-lay”] proposed its six-sided ring in 1865.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this flat, ring-shaped hydrocarbon made of six carbon atoms and six hydrogen atoms, the simplest aromatic compound.

tossups.p: Eilhard Mitscherlich [“MIT-sher-likh”] made this compound in 1833 by heating an acid from a tree resin with lime. Eight years earlier, Michael Faraday had found it in the oily residue left over from making gas for lamps and called it “bicarburet of hydrogen.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this six-carbon ring compound, the simplest aromatic hydrocarbon, whose ring August Kekulé proposed.

tossups.p: At an 1890 celebration in honor of his work on this compound, a chemist said he had found its structure after dozing by a fire and dreaming of a snake seizing its own tail. That chemist’s structures draw this compound with alternating single and double bonds.
tossups.r: That chemist was August Kekulé. For 10 points, name this hydrocarbon whose six carbon atoms form a flat hexagon.

tossups.p: All six carbon–carbon bonds in this compound have the same length, between that of a single bond and a double bond, because its electrons are spread around the whole ring. It is often drawn as a hexagon with a circle inside.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this aromatic compound, whose two Kekulé [“KAY-kuh-lay”] structures are resonance forms.

tossups.p: A rule by Erich Hückel [“HOO-kul”] says a flat ring with 4n + 2 pi electrons is especially stable, and this compound, with six pi electrons, is the classic example. Those electrons form clouds of charge above and below the plane of its carbon atoms.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this simplest aromatic hydrocarbon, which has six carbon atoms in a hexagonal ring.

tossups.p: Adding hydrogen to this compound releases about 150 kilojoules per mole less heat than expected for three ordinary double bonds, a measure of its extra stability called resonance energy. Fully adding hydrogen turns it into cyclohexane, which is used to make nylon.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this stable, ring-shaped hydrocarbon, the parent compound of the aromatic family.

tossups.p: Instead of adding atoms across its double bonds, this compound usually undergoes substitution, keeping its ring intact; for example, a mix of nitric and sulfuric acids swaps one of its hydrogens for a nitro group. Unlike alkenes, it does not turn bromine water colorless.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this aromatic hydrocarbon whose molecules are hexagons of six carbon atoms.

tossups.p: Charles Friedel and James Crafts discovered reactions that attach alkyl or acyl groups to this compound, using aluminum chloride as a catalyst. Adding a methyl group to this compound gives toluene, and adding an –OH group gives phenol.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this simplest aromatic compound, a ring of six carbon atoms.

tossups.p: When two groups are attached to this compound’s ring, their positions are called ortho, meta, or para, depending on whether the groups are next to each other, one carbon apart, or directly across the ring. Removing one hydrogen from this compound gives a phenyl group.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this six-carbon ring compound, the simplest aromatic hydrocarbon, which Michael Faraday discovered.

tossups.p: The phenyl group’s name comes from a Greek word meaning “to shine,” because this compound was first found in gas burned for lighting. The amino acid phenylalanine contains a ring based on this compound.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this aromatic hydrocarbon discovered by Michael Faraday, whose six carbon atoms form a hexagon.

tossups.p: Long exposure to this compound can cause leukemia, so safer solvents such as toluene took its place in many labs and factories. This compound is a natural part of crude oil and gasoline.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this colorless, flammable liquid hydrocarbon, whose six carbon atoms form a flat hexagon with one hydrogen on each corner.

tossups.p: Industry turns most of this compound into styrene for polystyrene, cumene for making phenol and acetone, and cyclohexane for making nylon. Chemists get most of this compound from crude oil, though it was once taken mainly from coal tar.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this aromatic hydrocarbon, whose molecule is a hexagon of six carbon atoms, each bonded to one hydrogen.

tossups.p: Naphthalene, the chemical in old-fashioned mothballs, is two of this compound’s rings fused together. Aspirin and acetaminophen, two common pain relievers, each contain one of this compound’s rings with other groups attached.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this simplest aromatic hydrocarbon, a flat ring of six carbon atoms discovered by Michael Faraday.

tossups.p: Albert Ladenburg proposed a prism-shaped structure for this compound, and a two-ring isomer of it is named for James Dewar. Both of those shapes turned out to be wrong for this compound, whose real shape is a flat hexagon.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this aromatic compound made of six carbon atoms and six hydrogen atoms.

tossups.p: Each carbon atom in this compound is sp2 hybridized, giving it bond angles of 120 degrees. This compound freezes at about 5.5 degrees Celsius and boils at about 80 degrees, and like other aromatic compounds it burns with a very smoky flame.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this flat, ring-shaped aromatic hydrocarbon first isolated by Michael Faraday in 1825.

Naphthalene, the chemical in old-fashioned mothballs, is two of its rings fused together
Wrong proposed shapes: Albert Ladenburg’s prism and a two-ring isomer named for James Dewar
Each carbon is sp2 hybridized with 120° bond angles; it freezes near 5.5 °C and boils near 80 °C
Long exposure can cause leukemia, so safer solvents like toluene took its place

trap.title: The ring, not its relatives
trap.body: Tossups on this compound mention many of its relatives: toluene (with a methyl group added), phenol (with an –OH group), styrene, and naphthalene (two rings fused together). Answering a relative is wrong when the question wants the plain six-carbon ring. Cyclohexane, the six-carbon ring with no double bonds, is another trap: it has twelve hydrogens and none of this compound’s special stability.
trap.fix: Six carbons and six hydrogens, Faraday, Kekulé’s snake dream, Hückel’s rule, and a circle drawn inside a hexagon mean this answer. If the question describes an extra group stuck onto the ring, it may want that derivative instead.
trap.line: Real answer line: Benzene (or C6H6; accept benzol; prompt on aromatic hydrocarbon or arene; do not accept “toluene” or other benzene derivatives)

topics.name: Lead (element)
topics.kicker: Element 82 · The soft, heavy metal of old pipes, paint, and batteries
topics.briefing: Lead is a soft, heavy, bluish-gray metal that people have used for thousands of years; the Romans made water pipes from it, and its Latin name, plumbum, gave us the word “plumbing.” Car batteries and the heavy aprons worn during X-rays still use it. Because lead is poisonous, especially to children, it was taken out of gasoline and house paint, and the “lead” in your pencil is really harmless graphite.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: The inert pair effect explains why this element’s +2 oxidation state is far more stable than its +4 state, unlike the lighter members of its group. This element’s most common isotope has a “doubly magic” nucleus, because both its number of protons and its number of neutrons are magic numbers.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this soft, heavy metal with atomic number 82, whose symbol comes from the Latin word plumbum.

tossups.p: Clair Patterson measured isotopes of this element in meteorites to calculate in 1956 that Earth is about 4.55 billion years old. During that work, Patterson discovered how much of this element people had spread into the environment, and he spent years campaigning to get it out of gasoline.
tossups.r: Uranium slowly decays into this element. For 10 points, name this toxic metal with atomic number 82.

tossups.p: Working for General Motors in 1921, Thomas Midgley Jr. found that a compound of this metal with four ethyl groups stopped car engines from “knocking.” The United States banned gasoline containing that compound for cars in 1996, because this metal is toxic.
tossups.r: This metal was also taken out of house paint. For 10 points, name this heavy metal with atomic number 82.

tossups.p: Gaston Planté [“plahn-TAY”] invented the first rechargeable battery in 1859 using sheets of this metal in sulfuric acid. In a car battery, plates of this metal and of its dioxide both turn into this metal’s sulfate as the battery runs down.
tossups.r: Its main ore is the mineral galena. For 10 points, name this dense metal with atomic number 82.

tossups.p: In 1746, John Roebuck began making sulfuric acid on a large scale inside huge chambers lined with sheets of this metal, which resists attack by that acid. Ancient Romans bent sheets of this soft metal into water pipes.
tossups.r: The word “plumbing” comes from this metal’s Latin name. For 10 points, name this heavy element with atomic number 82.

tossups.p: Alchemists linked this metal with the planet Saturn, so poisoning by it was once called “saturnism.” For centuries, artists painted with a white pigment made from a carbonate of this metal, until safer titanium and zinc whites mostly replaced it.
tossups.r: This metal was banned from U.S. house paint in 1978. For 10 points, name this element with atomic number 82.

tossups.p: Below about 7 kelvins, this metal becomes a superconductor that carries electric current with no resistance. Because it melts at only about 327 degrees Celsius, this soft, dense metal is easy to cast into fishing sinkers and the heavy weights in sailboat keels.
tossups.r: Aprons containing this metal protect patients during X-rays. For 10 points, name this element with atomic number 82.

tossups.p: Ancient Athens paid for its warships with silver from the mines at Laurium, where the silver was separated from ores of this metal. Early “crystal radio” sets used a thin wire touching a cube-shaped crystal of galena, a sulfide of this metal.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this toxic metal, whose chemical symbol comes from the Latin word plumbum.

tossups.p: After Flint, Michigan, switched its water source in 2014 without treating the water to control corrosion, this metal began dissolving from old pipes into people’s tap water. Health agencies say there is no known safe level of this metal in a child’s blood.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this toxic heavy metal, which was also removed from gasoline and house paint.

tossups.p: The uranium-238 decay series ends with this element’s stable isotope of mass number 206, and the thorium-232 series ends with its isotope of mass number 208. Geologists measure uranium and this element in tiny zircon crystals to find the ages of ancient rocks.
tossups.r: This metal is used in car batteries. For 10 points, name this heavy metal with atomic number 82.

tossups.p: Flerovium, element 114, sits directly below this element on the periodic table. Traditional solder for joining wires and pipes is an alloy of tin and this element, which sits just below tin in the carbon group.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this soft, toxic metal that ancient Romans used to make water pipes.

tossups.p: The word “miniature” comes from minium, a bright red oxide of this metal that medieval artists used to decorate handwritten books. That same red oxide was later painted onto iron and steel to keep them from rusting.
tossups.r: Its main ore is galena. For 10 points, name this heavy metal with atomic number 82.

tossups.p: In the 1670s, George Ravenscroft developed a sparkling English glass that gets its brilliance from an oxide of this metal. Thick windows made of that same kind of glass let scientists safely watch radioactive materials.
tossups.r: Aprons containing this metal protect patients from X-rays. For 10 points, name this dense, poisonous element with atomic number 82.

tossups.p: Graphite was once called plumbago because people mistook it for an ore of this metal. That old mistake is why the gray core of a pencil is still named after this metal, even though pencils contain none of it.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this toxic heavy metal, whose chemical symbol comes from the Latin word plumbum.

tossups.p: Mixing solutions of potassium iodide and a nitrate of this metal makes a bright yellow solid. When that solid dissolves in hot water and then cools, it forms glittering flakes nicknamed “golden rain.”
tossups.r: This metal sits just below tin in group 14. For 10 points, name this element with atomic number 82.

trap.title: Not graphite, not tin
trap.body: Pencil cores carry this element’s name, but they are really graphite, a form of carbon, so a tossup about pencils or plumbago may want graphite or carbon instead. Tin is the other trap: it sits just above this element in group 14, and the two metals were mixed together in solder and pewter. Mercury, another toxic heavy metal, also tempts early buzzers.
trap.fix: Atomic number 82, plumbum, galena, car batteries, X-ray aprons, and old gasoline and paint point here. Tin is element 50 (its symbol, Sn, comes from stannum) and coats “tin cans”; mercury is the liquid metal in old thermometers.

topics.name: Fluorine
topics.kicker: Element 9 · The most reactive and most electronegative element
topics.briefing: Fluorine is the wildest element on the periodic table: this pale yellow gas reacts with almost everything, and it pulls on electrons harder than any other atom. It was so dangerous to isolate that chemists tried for decades before Henri Moissan finally succeeded in 1886. Tamed in compounds, it is everywhere: fluoride in toothpaste fights cavities, and nonstick Teflon pans are coated with a plastic made of carbon and fluorine.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Several chemists were poisoned or injured in failed attempts to isolate this element before Henri Moissan [“mwah-SAHN”] finally succeeded in 1886, using electrolysis in a chilled platinum apparatus. Moissan won the 1906 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for that work.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this pale yellow gas, the lightest halogen and the most electronegative element.

tossups.p: In an 1812 letter to Humphry Davy, André-Marie Ampère [“ahm-PAIR”] suggested a name for this element, decades before anyone managed to isolate it. A mineral made of calcium and this element defines a hardness of 4 on the Mohs scale.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this element with atomic number 9, whose ion, fluoride, is added to toothpaste.

tossups.p: While working on refrigerant gases at DuPont in 1938, Roy Plunkett accidentally discovered a slippery plastic made of carbon and this element. Carbon bonds to this element so strongly that compounds called PFAS, which contain many such bonds, are nicknamed “forever chemicals.”
tossups.r: That plastic, Teflon, coats nonstick pans. For 10 points, name this most electronegative element, the lightest halogen.

tossups.p: This element has an oxidation number of −1 in all of its compounds, and in its compounds with oxygen, it even forces oxygen into a positive oxidation state. Atoms of this element are the smallest of all the halogens.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this element with atomic number 9, the most reactive halogen.

tossups.p: During the Manhattan Project, uranium was enriched by turning it into a gas of uranium and this element, a method helped by the fact that this element has only one natural isotope. A radioactive isotope of this element with mass number 18 is used in medical PET scans.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this lightest halogen, whose ion is added to toothpaste to fight cavities.

tossups.p: Xenon can bond to two, four, or six atoms of this element, and krypton also forms a compound with it. Neil Bartlett’s 1962 discovery that noble gases can form compounds used a compound of platinum and this element.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this pale yellow gas with atomic number 9, the most electronegative element.

tossups.p: Surprisingly, the bond holding two atoms of this element together is weaker than the bond in a chlorine molecule, because this element’s tiny atoms crowd their lone pairs close enough to repel. Chlorine also beats this element in electron affinity.
tossups.r: Even so, this element tops Linus Pauling’s electronegativity scale. For 10 points, name this lightest halogen, element number 9.

tossups.p: In 1945, Grand Rapids, Michigan, became the first city to add a compound of this element to its drinking water to prevent tooth decay. Dentists sometimes paint a varnish containing this element onto children’s teeth for the same reason.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this element whose −1 ion, fluoride, is found in most toothpastes.

tossups.p: Even though this element is extremely reactive, its compound with hydrogen forms only a weak acid in water. That acid can etch glass, so it must be stored in plastic bottles, and it is used to etch frosted designs onto glassware.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this element with atomic number 9, the lightest member of the halogens.

tossups.p: Aluminum is made by dissolving its oxide in molten cryolite, a mineral of sodium, aluminum, and this element that was once mined in Greenland. A heavy, nonflammable gas made of sulfur and this element insulates high-voltage electrical equipment.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this pale yellow halogen with atomic number 9, the most electronegative element.

tossups.p: Thomas Midgley Jr. helped develop refrigerant gases containing carbon, chlorine, and this element, which were later found to damage the ozone layer. The 1987 Montreal Protocol phased out those gases, called CFCs.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this element with atomic number 9, which sits just above chlorine in group 17.

tossups.p: Hydrogen gas explodes on contact with this element even in the dark and at very low temperatures, unlike a mixture of hydrogen and chlorine, which needs light to set it off. This element forms compounds with nearly every other element.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this most reactive element, a pale yellow halogen with atomic number 9.

tossups.p: This element’s ion can take the place of hydroxide ions in hydroxyapatite, the mineral that makes up tooth enamel. That swap makes enamel harder for the acids made by mouth bacteria to dissolve, which helps prevent cavities.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this element, whose −1 ion, fluoride, is added to most toothpastes.

tossups.p: This element holds its electrons so tightly that it has the highest first ionization energy of any halogen. Its atoms have the electron configuration 1s² 2s² 2p⁵, one electron short of the next element, neon.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this element with atomic number 9, which forms diatomic molecules of a pale yellow gas.

tossups.p: This element’s name comes from the Latin word for “flow,” because a mineral containing it was added to metal ores to help them melt and flow. That mineral, a compound of calcium and this element, comes in many colors, including purple and green.
tossups.r: The word “fluorescence” also comes from that mineral’s name. For 10 points, name this element with atomic number 9.

The most electronegative element, with a value of nearly 4 on Pauling’s scale
The most reactive element; it forms compounds with nearly every other element

A pale yellow gas made of diatomic molecules
Teflon, the nonstick coating on pans, is a plastic made of carbon and this element

trap.title: Element, not fluoride
trap.body: Many clues are really about fluoride, this element’s −1 ion, in toothpaste and tap water, so players blurt “fluoride” or the mineral “fluorite.” Those are different answers: the tossup wants the element itself. Chlorine is the other trap, since the two halogens share clues about reactivity, CFCs, and diatomic gases.
trap.fix: If it asks for “this element,” name the element, not its ion or its mineral. Atomic number 9, pale yellow, most electronegative, Moissan, and Teflon point here; chlorine is element 17, a yellow-green gas used to disinfect swimming pools.
trap.line: Real answer line: Fluorine (accept F; do not accept “fluoride”)
